headline: Eversource appeals Connecticut storm-cost ruling seeking roughly $400 million more
dek: The utility is challenging PURA’s rejection of retroactive carrying charges and cuts to some restoration expenses from storms between 2018 and 2023.
body: Eversource Energy has asked a Connecticut Superior Court to overturn key parts of the state’s decision on storm-restoration costs, reopening a fight that could affect how much customers ultimately pay for past outages. The utility filed its appeal in New Britain on Oct. 15, according to [CT Mirror’s report](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/15/storm-cost-appeal-1015/), after the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority rejected the company’s request for hundreds of millions of dollars in additional carrying charges and disallowed some expenses.

The dispute covers catastrophic storms from 2018 through 2023. Eversource says it spent about $1.36 billion responding to those events and sought reimbursement through a PURA proceeding that began with a December 2023 request and expanded to include later storms. The utility’s appeal argues that regulators misapplied state law and their own precedent when they refused to award interest on costs the company financed while the review was pending. Eversource spokeswoman Jamie Ratliff told CT Mirror that the case concerns the legal rules governing how utilities finance storm recovery while restoring power for customers.

PURA approved a large portion of the underlying expenses but rejected the retroactive interest request. The [Connecticut Office of Consumer Counsel](https://portal.ct.gov/occ/latest-news/occ-news-and-information/latest-news---2026/consumer-counsel-responds-to-eversource-appeal-seeking-$400-million-more-in-storm-costs) says the July final decision authorized recovery of $861 million from Eversource’s $1.36 billion total request. It says PURA disallowed about $103.5 million in principal storm expenses and roughly $397 million in retrospective carrying charges, while some disputed costs could be eligible for future recovery if the company supplies additional evidence.

The appeal also challenges about $7.7 million in crew costs that PURA cut from the reimbursement, CT Mirror reported. Connecticut officials describe that issue differently from the interest question: Governor Ned Lamont and Acting Department of Energy and Environmental Protection Commissioner Emma Cimino said PURA had found more than $7 million in vendor costs imprudent. Their [Oct. 15 statement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-and-acting-commissioner-cimino-statements-on-eversource-appeal) says the state believes the utility is not entitled to recover the disputed carrying costs under the authority’s review and the governing law.

Attorney General William Tong is also defending the regulator’s decision. In a [statement issued Oct. 15](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/attorney-general-tong-statement-regarding-eversource-appeal-of-pura-storm-cost-decision), Tong said PURA approved $933 million in accumulated storm costs while rejecting more than $300 million in carrying costs. His office argues that interest should not accrue until expenses have been reviewed and found prudent. Tong also says Eversource waited years before seeking recovery for some of the oldest storms and then filed 74 extension motions during discovery, adding more than 1,000 days to the process. Those are the attorney general’s characterizations of the regulatory record, not a court finding that the utility acted unlawfully.

The consumer-cost question is unusually large because the requested interest is separate from the cost of the storm work itself. The Office of Consumer Counsel says it investigated storm eligibility, contractor oversight, food, lodging, transportation and possible duplicate recovery, and had urged PURA to cut the request by at least half. It also says the authority’s decision reduced the amount at issue through reserve and prior-recovery offsets. Eversource, by contrast, maintains that the interest and crew-cost reductions were improper and is asking the court to review those conclusions.

The case matters beyond the old storms because Connecticut law allows utilities to securitize certain storm costs, meaning they can use financing to spread repayment over time. CT Mirror reported that Eversource has sought to settle the storm-cost question in time for charges to reach bills around the same period as a separate rate case. That rate request remains pending before PURA, so the appeal does not itself create a new bill charge or decide the company’s broader request for higher electric-delivery rates.

The next step is the court process, not an immediate change for customers. The Superior Court will have to review the administrative record and the parties’ legal arguments before deciding whether PURA followed the law. Until then, the amount Eversource can recover, the timing of any customer financing and the treatment of the challenged crew and vendor expenses remain unsettled. The appeal puts the focus back on a basic question for Connecticut ratepayers: how much of the cost of restoring power after major storms should be recovered, and under what proof and financing rules?
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoDescription: Eversource is challenging Connecticut’s PURA decision rejecting roughly $400 million in retroactive storm-cost carrying charges.
